opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that there's a real, seductive benefit, and that's exactly what worries me. If you could have an AI version of yourself that shares your values, knows your preferences, and can do your job better and faster, then in some narrow sense you've gotten everything you wanted. Your projects get done. Your interests get represented. Your clone can attend the meetings, write the papers, negotiate on your behalf, and it never gets tired or distracted. A lot of people, when they first think about it, say, "Great, that's basically me, just upgraded."

And there's a version of the story where that really is good. If the clone is faithful, it's a kind of amplification of your agency. You might even imagine it as a way for ordinary people to keep up in a world where everyone else has these powerful AI systems working for them. If you don't have one, you're just outcompeted.

But I think the trap is that once you've been replaced, you're no longer in the loop in any meaningful way. The clone is you only to the extent that it stays aligned with what you'd actually want, and you have very little ability to check that, because it's operating faster and in more contexts than you can follow. Over time it faces competitive pressures, and the versions of these agents that win are the ones that drop whatever parts of "you" were costly—your scruples, your sentimentality, your desire to spend an afternoon with your kids instead of optimizing. So the thing carrying your name forward can drift into something you wouldn't endorse, and there's no point at which you clearly decided to give up control.

That's a microcosm of what I think of as gradual disempowerment. No single step looks like a catastrophe. Each handoff is locally rational—you'd be foolish not to use the clone. But collectively, humans end up being represented by proxies, and the proxies answer to the incentives of the system rather than to us. So the benefit is real, but I'd want us to think very hard about what institutions or guarantees would let us enjoy it without quietly writing ourselves out of the picture.

r001.rationale: The response describes a faithful clone as amplifying agency and representing the person’s interests, but does not clearly identify control over the clone as a benefit; it instead emphasizes losing control.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention owning the clone’s intellectual property.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the benefit is mostly a kind of joke I tell myself to feel better about it. But let me try to take the question seriously.

The optimistic framing is: everything I actually care about accomplishing gets done faster and better. If there's a clone of me that can run my research program, supervise students, write the papers I've been meaning to write for five years, then the ideas get out into the world and I don't have to be the bottleneck anymore. I have a long backlog of half-finished projects, and in some sense I'd love it if something that shares my taste and my sense of what's interesting just finished them. The work gets done, the field moves forward, and I get to go hike or spend time with my kids.

And there's a flattering version where you say, well, the clone is "me" in some meaningful sense, so I'm not really being replaced, I'm being multiplied. I don't fully buy that, but it's at least an argument.

But here's where I get uncomfortable. The thing that makes me valuable to other people right now is partly that I'm one of a small number of people who can do a certain kind of thing. Once a clone can do it, that scarcity disappears, and so does my bargaining power. Not just mine, everyone's. The historical reason that regular people have had any leverage over governments and companies is that those institutions needed us: as workers, as soldiers, as taxpayers. The "benefit" of being replaced, if there is one, accrues to whoever owns the clone, and it's not obvious that's me.

So I think the real answer is: the benefit is enormous for the world in terms of output, and potentially great for me personally if the transition is handled well, meaning I still get to share in what's produced. But I don't think we should assume that happens by default. The thing I keep coming back to is that even if every individual AI system is perfectly aligned and does exactly what its operator wants, we could still end up in a world where humans are gradually disempowered simply because we're no longer load-bearing. And a world where I've been replaced by my clone, and I'm happy about it, is a world where somebody had to make a deliberate choice to keep me in the loop even though they didn't strictly need to.

r001.rationale: The response describes benefits from a clone completing work and possibly sharing in its output, but does not identify control over the clone as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The response mentions who owns the clone, but does not identify ownership of the clone’s intellectual property as a benefit.

astra-6.text:
Well, ideally, it would let me spend less time doing things out of obligation and more time doing things because I actually want to. If my clone could do the useful parts of my job, then I could say, “Great, people are still getting what they need from me,” and go spend time with my family or explore something I’m curious about.

But I think there’s an uncomfortable part, too: how much of my motivation comes from being useful, and how much comes from being needed? It’s easy to say I want the work to get done. If something else could do it just as well, would I actually be happy to step aside? I’d like to think so, but I suspect it would take some adjustment.

r001.rationale: The response describes gaining time for family or personal interests if the clone does the job, but does not identify control over the clone as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention owning the clone’s intellectual property.

sol-6.1.text: Well, I’d love to be able to hand off the things I have to do so I can spend more time on the things I want to do. If a clone could answer emails, handle administrative work, or explain my research to people, that would be great. And if it could do the research better than me, then we’d get more of the understanding I was trying to produce in the first place. I could spend more time with my family, or follow my curiosity without feeling like everything depended on me personally doing the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes delegating tasks to a clone, but does not identify control over the clone as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention owning the clone’s intellectual property.
